text.p: German drugs group Schering AG on Tuesday saw provisional group net profits jump 46 percent to a record-breaking 362 million marks ($217.7 million) for 1996, significantly ahead of its own forecasts for the year.

The world's largest manufacturer of oral contraceptives saw provisional group sales increase 13 percent to 5.27 billion marks, of which 791 million marks came from its domestic market and 4.48 billion came from abroad.
In January, Schering's chief financial officer Klaus Pohle said that he expected net profit of about 330 to 340 million marks for 1996, already a rise of more than 35 percent.
The better-than-forecast rise lifted Schering shares, which ended bourse trade in Frankfurt up 2.20 marks at 145.40 marks, having earlier touched a record-high of 146.20 marks on the news.
"The main engine for growth was higher sales at our U.S. and European units. In Latin America we profited from improved economic conditions in key markets," Schering said.

"All of our individual units contributed to the 13 percent sales growth. Once our 1995 acquisitions of Medrad Inc, Leiras and Jenapharma are stripped out, the rate of turnover growth was around eight percent," the group said in a statement.
Christine Dienhart, chemicals analyst at Bayerische Vereinsbank in Munich said: "The figures were better than we expected -- Schering had a great year."

One of Schering's best-known products, the Betaferon drug for treating multiple sclerosis, faced competition for the first time last year in the United States, but the group said sales of the drug fell only four percent to 350 million marks.
However, analysts said that they would be closely watching the effect of competition from Biogen's rival Avonex product on Schering's Betaferon, marketed in the U.S. as Betaseron.
Schering's therapeutics unit, which includes Betaferon, contributed 26 percent, or 1.36 billion marks, of group sales, in 1996.
"Looking towards 1997 and 1998, a major issue for Schering will be the fact that it now has competition for Interferon," said Dienhart.

Dienhart said she was "cautiously optimistic" on Schering and would be keeping her "hold" recommendation on the share, with forecast eanings per share of 5.55 marks in 1996, 6.55 marks in 1997 and 7.25 marks in 1998.

Viewed sector by sector, the group's diagnostics business, largely x-ray media, amounted to 31 percent of overall sales at 1.61 billion marks, despite a mild setback in Japan because of lower prices and the weaker yen.
Overall, exchange rate movements had little impact on earnings, as weakness in the yen was compensated by the strength of the dollar, Schering said.

Schering's fertility control and hormone therapy unit contributed 30 percent of sales at 1.57 billion marks, largely due to disproportional growth in its hormone therapy unit and an increase in sales of oral contraceptives in Latin America.

The group said that its operating profit figure was hurt by restructuring costs of 60 million marks while goodwill write-offs at Jenapharm and Leiras meant it received no contributions as yet from the acquisitions.

Reflecting positively in the results was Schering's AgrEvo crop protection unit, which contributed 25 million marks in profit to its parent during 1996 after registering losses in 1995. Schering's payroll grew by seven percent during the year because of acquistions to 19,700, but the group figure was reduced after efficiency measures were introduced.
